layers.title: Lawsuits by commercial creditors against this government over unpaid debt, filed 1976 to 2010
layers.plain: How many banks, funds and other professional lenders took this government to court or arbitration over debt it had stopped paying. A creditor's repeat suits against one government count once, even if it filed many. This is a total across 1976 to 2010, not a yearly number. The authors searched courts in the US and UK and international arbitration only, and left out small private investors, so a blank means none found under those rules, not that none ever happened.
layers.source: Schumacher, Trebesch and Enderlein, Sovereign Defaults in Court, 2018 litigation database
layers.how: All 158 rows of the published spreadsheet, counted by debtor country. How the source defines a lawsuit (ECB Working Paper 2135, section 3 and Appendix 4): a dispute filed by a foreign commercial creditor (hedge fund, bank or other professional investor) against a sovereign government, or against a public body whose debt it guaranteed, in a US or UK court or an international arbitration tribunal, over marketable debt (bonds, loans, promissory notes, guarantees) in default between 1975 and 2010. Repeat suits by one creditor against one government merge into one row, even across courts: NML Capital filed more than 10 actions against Argentina and counts once. A row can also hold several plaintiffs suing together. Argentina saw 182 lawsuits in the Southern District of New York alone. Excluded: retail investors (83 such US or UK cases; 241 in all if included), expropriation and war-reparation claims, procurement bills, and defaults from before the period such as Russian tsarist bonds. Absence: the file lists 34 countries. A country not listed had no case found under those rules; courts elsewhere and later years were not covered. Blank is not zero. Argentina has 52 rows: the paper text says 50, and its Table 1 shows those 50 are the cases after the 2001 default (158 total, 108 without them); the file holds two earlier ones (Weltover 1989, Sayal 1992). Totals, outcome, jurisdiction and decade counts match Table 1. Year_first and year_last are filing years, read from all date forms in the file; one case (Trendtex v. Nigeria) was filed 4 November 1975, before the 1976 start the paper states. End dates and amounts run later: pending cases are as of end-2016. Amounts sum the face value, amount claimed and judgment columns in millions of US dollars where filled. A "." in the file means not given; where every case for a country is ".", the field is null, not 0, and cases_with_face, cases_with_claimed and cases_with_judgment show how many cases have a figure. Likewise attachment_attempts is null where the file gives no answer for any case; an attachment attempt is a motion to seize assets or block payments. Outcomes use the file's labels; the paper defines OCS as out-of-court settlement, and not_stated is the file's ".". Later cases 2011-2018 appear only as case studies in the paper and are not in the file.

layers.title: Money awarded to commercial creditors against this government, cases filed 1976 to 2010
layers.plain: The US dollars that courts and arbitrators ordered this government to pay in those lawsuits. This is a total across cases filed 1976 to 2010, added as published with no inflation adjustment. An award is not money paid: some cases later settled and some remain unpaid. Many cases have no figure, so the total can be too low, and a blank country means the file gives no figure, not zero.
layers.source: Schumacher, Trebesch and Enderlein, Sovereign Defaults in Court, 2018 litigation database
layers.how: Sum of the Judgment amount (USD m) column, converted from millions to whole US dollars and rounded to the nearest 10,000. The paper defines it as the damage as determined by the final judgment. Total 5,507.71 million across 19 countries. Of 158 cases, 96 have a figure and 62 have "." (not given), which adds nothing and is not treated as zero; 10 have a real 0 in the file, which is counted as 0. No country has only zeros. Fifteen countries have no figure on any case and are left out: blank, not zero. The column includes 19 cases the file marks Pending (687.52 million) and 5 it marks Unsuccessful (93.68 million), so the total does not equal money recovered. cases counts all cases for the country; cases_with_figure and cases_no_figure split them. Definitions of a lawsuit and what absence means are in the lawsuit-count layer.

layers.title: Times this country restructured debt with private lenders, 1970 to 2013
layers.plain: How many times this government struck a deal with foreign banks and bondholders to reduce or delay repayment because it could not pay as agreed. This is a total across 1970 to 2013, not a yearly number. Deals with other governments, deals mainly with lenders at home and routine refinancing are not counted, so a blank means none found under those rules. The 1823 to 2024 layer covers the same years in part, so do not add the two.
layers.source: Cruces and Trebesch, Sovereign Defaults: The Price of Haircuts, 2014 update
layers.how: All 187 deals in the sheet "2014 Version (new)", counted by the sheet's country code. How the source defines a restructuring: a distressed exchange of public or government-guaranteed medium or long-term debt with foreign banks or bondholders, on terms worse for the lender than the original, and actually carried out. Excluded: debt owed to other governments including the Paris Club, debt mainly held at home (two exceptions, Russia 1998 GKOs and Ukraine 1998 OVDPs, mainly held by foreigners), routine swaps and buybacks, short-term rollovers, extensions under a year, private-to-private workouts, and deals never completed. Absence: a country not listed had no deal found that meets these rules. It does not mean the country never defaulted or never restructured other debts. The earliest deal in the sheet is 1978. Each row is one deal, so a country with bank and bond deals can have two in one year; years lists one entry per deal. debt_restructured_usd_m sums the published column in current US dollars of each deal's year, not adjusted for inflation. Yugoslavia keeps the sheet's code YUG, flagged because it is no longer a country and has no current map shape; SRB here is only the 2004 Serbia and Montenegro deal. Overlap: this period is also covered by the 1823-2024 layer, which has 174 deals in 1970-2013 against 187 here, since some deals are merged or left out and some haircuts differ. Use one layer at a time and do not add them.

layers.title: Average share private lenders lost in this government's debt deals, 1970 to 2013
layers.plain: The average share of their money's value that foreign banks and bondholders gave up in this government's debt deals from 1970 to 2013. It counts cuts to the amount owed plus value lost to lower interest and longer waits. This is one average across all those years, and it is this map's own calculation from the authors' deal-by-deal figures, with larger deals counting more. A negative number means lenders came out ahead. A lender caught in several deals in a row could lose more than this.
layers.source: Cruces and Trebesch, Sovereign Defaults: The Price of Haircuts, 2014 update
layers.how: n is this map's own calculation, not a published figure: each deal's Preferred Haircut HSZ multiplied by its Debt Restructured, added up, divided by the country's total Debt Restructured, as a percent. simple_mean_pct (every deal equal) and max_pct are also calculated here from the same rows. The authors publish haircuts deal by deal only. HSZ compares the present value of the old debt with that of the new debt at the same discount rate; the sheet also publishes a Market Haircut, not used. Weights are current US dollars of each deal's year, since this file has no inflation-adjusted column, so later, larger deals pull the average most. The weighted average is sound as a size-adjusted summary of deals, but it is not a cumulative loss: the same debt can be restructured repeatedly, and the average does not compound those losses. Seven deals have negative haircuts (Brazil 1983, Mexico 1983, Nigeria 1984, Peru 1978 and 1980, Ukraine 1999, Yugoslavia 1984), meaning the new terms were worth more than the old; they are kept. Absence: a country not listed had no deal found that meets these rules. It does not mean the country never defaulted or never restructured other debts. Definitions and codes are in the 1970-2013 count layer.

layers.title: Times this country restructured debt with private lenders, 1823 to 2024
layers.plain: How many deals this country has on record with foreign private lenders to reduce or delay repayment, or outright refusals to pay, added up over 1823 to 2024. This is a total across all those years, not a yearly number. Deals with other governments and deals never completed are not counted, so a blank means none found under those rules. It overlaps the 1970 to 2013 layer, and the two do not match exactly, so do not add them.
layers.source: Graf von Luckner, Meyer, Reinhart and Trebesch, Sovereign Haircuts: 200 Years of Creditor Losses
layers.how: All 329 rows of the sheet "Individual Restructurings", counted by the sheet's country code. How the source defines a restructuring: a completed distressed exchange of government or government-guaranteed medium or long-term external debt with private creditors, on terms worse for the lender; full repudiations (9 rows, flagged in the file and carried as full_repudiations) are included with a 100 percent haircut. Absence: a country not listed has no such case in this dataset, which is not proof of none. Overlap: the sheet has 174 deals dated 1970-2013 against 187 in the 1970-2013 layer. It is not a simple superset. Some deals there are merged or missing here (for example Brazil 1992, Mozambique 2007, Panama 1994), Zimbabwe 1980 appears only here, and the four YUG deals there sit here as three under SRB. Codes: CZK is the source's own code for Czechoslovakia, not an ISO3 country code (it is the code for the Czech koruna; the old ISO code was CSK), flagged because it has no current map shape. SRB in this sheet covers Yugoslavia (1895, 1967, 1984, 1985, 1988) and Serbia and Montenegro (2004), so it is not comparable with SRB in the 1970-2013 layer. Earlier states sit under the source's code, for example Russia 1917 under RUS. Likely source errors, kept as published and not filtered: Pakistan has two identical rows with Case ID 17 (777.2 million, 11.6 percent), where the 1970-2013 layer has a bank deal and a separate 610 million bond deal; Russia has two identical 1,307 million rows for 2000, where the 1970-2013 layer also has a 31,943 million deal; Poland has two identical 1,957 million rows for 1982, where the 1970-2013 layer has a 1982 deal of 2,225 million at 62.9 percent. One Ukraine row (2016) has a blank repudiation mark, counted as not a repudiation. debt_restructured_usd_m_current sums dollars of each deal's year, so old and recent deals are not comparable; debt_restructured_usd_m_real_2020 sums the published 2020-dollar column.

layers.title: Average share private lenders lost in this country's debt deals, 1823 to 2024
layers.plain: The average share of their money's value that foreign private lenders gave up in this country's debt deals from 1823 to 2024. It counts cuts to the amount owed plus value lost to lower interest and longer waits. This is one average across all those years, and it is this map's own calculation from the authors' deal-by-deal figures, with larger deals counting more after adjusting for inflation. A negative number means lenders came out ahead. A lender caught in several deals in a row could lose more than this.
layers.source: Graf von Luckner, Meyer, Reinhart and Trebesch, Sovereign Haircuts: 200 Years of Creditor Losses
layers.how: n is this map's own calculation, not a published figure: each deal's Net-Present-Value Haircut multiplied by its Debt Restructured in 2020 US dollars, added up, divided by the country's total, as a percent. 2020 dollars are used because the layer spans two centuries, and current dollars would let a 1990s dollar count the same as a far more valuable 1890s dollar; the current-dollar version is kept as current_dollar_weighted_pct and simple_mean_pct gives every deal equal weight. max_pct is also calculated here. The authors publish haircuts deal by deal, and cumulative Bulow-Rogoff haircuts per default spell in the sheet Default Spells, which are not carried here. Their read-me warns that simple averages overweight interim low-haircut deals, so this average is a size-adjusted summary of deals, not a cumulative loss. Full repudiations count as 100 percent. Negative haircuts are kept. Five rows show a 0 haircut, kept as published but flagged: China 1937 and Yugoslavia 1967 and Zimbabwe 1980 pair it with a face value cut, which is odd, and Poland 1938 and Russia 1997 show 0 on both. Russia 1997 matters most: 30,500 million at 0 percent here against 26.2 percent for the same 1997 deal in the 1970-2013 layer, which lowers Russia's average here, and the Zimbabwe figure of 0 rests only on its one row. Quote those flagged countries with care. Definitions, codes, overlap and likely source errors are in the 1823-2024 count layer.
